lessons.title: Body structure: cells, skeleton and muscles
lessons.html:
Anatomy and physiology

Anatomy is the study of the parts of the body and where they are. Physiology is the study of how those parts work. A stockman who understands both can handle animals better, spot illness sooner and give injections in the right place.

From cells to systems

  • Cells are the smallest living units of the body.
  • Cells of the same kind form tissues, such as muscle, bone, nerve and skin.
  • Tissues form organs, such as the heart, liver and kidneys.
  • Organs that work together form systems, such as the digestive or reproductive system.

The skeleton

The skeleton supports the body, protects organs and works with muscles to move the animal. Important parts include:

  • The skull, which protects the brain.
  • The spine (vertebrae) from neck to tail, which protects the spinal cord.
  • The ribs, which protect the heart and lungs.
  • The legs, with joints such as the hock, knee and fetlock. Cattle and sheep walk on two toes (cloven hooves); horses walk on one.

Bones need calcium and phosphorus. Young animals short of these minerals grow weak, bent bones.

Muscles

Muscles move the body by contracting. There are three kinds:

  1. Skeletal muscle - attached to bones and under the animal's control. This is the meat of the carcass.
  2. Smooth muscle - in the gut, bladder and blood vessels; works automatically.
  3. Heart muscle - beats non-stop throughout life.

Knowing where big muscles lie matters for injections. Intramuscular injections in cattle are usually given in the neck muscle, not in the rump, to avoid damaging valuable meat cuts. Always follow the product label and the vet's instructions for the injection site.

lessons.title: Digestion, breathing and circulation
lessons.html:
The digestive system

The digestive system takes in feed, breaks it down and absorbs the nutrients. Feed passes through the mouth, oesophagus (gullet), stomach, small intestine, large intestine and out through the anus.

  • In ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) the stomach has four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Microbes in the rumen break down grass fibre.
  • In monogastrics (pigs, poultry) there is one simple stomach. Poultry also have a crop for storage and a gizzard that grinds feed with grit.
  • The liver makes bile, stores energy and removes poisons.
  • The small intestine is where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood.

The respiratory system

Air enters through the nose, passes down the trachea (windpipe) into the lungs. In the lungs, oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out. Fast or noisy breathing, coughing and nasal discharge can mean pneumonia, which often follows stress, dust or cold, wet weather. Good ventilation in sheds and transport prevents many lung problems.

The circulatory system

The heart pumps blood through arteries to the body and back through veins. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones and white blood cells that fight infection. It also carries heat, which helps control body temperature.

Normal values to know

Every species has a normal range for temperature, pulse and breathing rate. Your vet or training manual will give you the normal ranges for the animals on your farm. Learn them, because a temperature well above normal usually means infection, and a temperature below normal in a weak animal is a serious warning sign. Take temperature with a thermometer in the rectum and record it.

lessons.title: Reproduction, nerves and other systems
lessons.html:
The reproductive system

Reproduction keeps the herd going, so it is central to farm income.

Female

  • Ovaries produce eggs and hormones.
  • Oviducts carry the egg; fertilisation happens here.
  • The uterus holds the growing foetus.
  • The cervix closes the uterus; the vagina and vulva lead to the outside.

Females come on heat (oestrus) in a regular cycle. In cows the cycle is about 21 days. Watch for heat signs and record them so animals can be served or inseminated on time.

Male

  • Testes in the scrotum produce sperm and the hormone testosterone. They hang outside the body because sperm needs a cooler temperature.
  • Sperm travels through ducts and is mixed with fluids from the accessory glands.

Bulls and rams should be checked for fertility before the breeding season.

The nervous system and senses

The brain, spinal cord and nerves control the body. Animals see, hear and smell well. Cattle have a wide field of view but a blind spot directly behind them, so never approach from behind where they cannot see you. Calm, quiet handling uses this knowledge to keep both people and animals safe.

Other systems

  • The urinary system (kidneys and bladder) removes waste. Blood in urine can mean redwater or other disease.
  • The skin, hair and wool protect the body and keep heat in. The mammary glands are specialised skin glands that produce milk.
  • The endocrine system makes hormones that control growth, milk and reproduction.

Key points

  • Anatomy is structure; physiology is how the body works.
  • Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.
  • Ruminants have a four-part stomach; pigs and poultry have a simple stomach.
  • Know normal temperature, pulse and breathing for your animals.
  • A cow's heat cycle is about 21 days; record heats.
